opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this comes out of work we did on what we called "forget-and-relearn," which built on a line of research around iterative training methods. People had noticed that if you take a network, train it for a while, then reset some of its weights, often the later layers, and keep training, you can end up with better generalization than if you'd just trained straight through. Knowledge evolution, for example, showed this in the few-shot setting. On the surface that's a bit puzzling: why would throwing away learned information help?

The way I've come to think about it is that forgetting is a selective pressure. When you reinitialize part of the network, you're disrupting what it has learned, but not uniformly. Some features are hard to destroy. They're robust, they're useful across many examples, and the rest of the network relies on them. Other features are fragile, like memorizing specific examples or latching onto idiosyncratic shortcuts. Those get wiped out more easily. Then in the relearning phase, the network has to rebuild, and the features that survived act as scaffolding. Over repeated cycles, you amplify the features that are consistently useful and easy to relearn, and you suppress the ones that weren't pulling their weight.

Why the later layers in particular? Earlier layers tend to learn more general, transferable features, things like edges and textures in vision, while later layers are more specialized and more prone to fitting the particulars of the training set. So if you reset the later layers, you keep the general representations intact and force the network to re-derive the more task-specific mapping on top of them. And because the early features are good, it can do that relatively quickly, ideally in a way that relies more on the shared structure and less on memorization.

So rather than seeing it as a quirky trick, I think of it as one instance of a broader framework: you have a forgetting step that removes undesirable information, and a relearning step that reinforces whatever information is consistently useful. That lens also connects it to other phenomena, like iterated learning in the study of language evolution, where repeated transmission through a bottleneck produces more compositional, more learnable structure. A lot of these seemingly different methods can be understood as shaping what the network ends up learning by controlling what it's allowed to keep.

r001.rationale: The response says robust, useful features survive and are reinforced through relearning, but does not identify continued strengthening of earlier-layer features as the experimentally favored explanation.

r002.rationale: It does not state that reinitializing later layers sends a stronger training signal back to earlier layers.

r003.rationale: It describes early features as general and transferable, but does not connect their generality to adapting readily across environments created by later-layer reinitializations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this came out of a paper we did called "Fortuitous Forgetting in Connectionist Networks," and the phenomenon you're describing is something people had noticed in a few different places. There's this "later layer forgetting" idea, and there's also related work like "born again networks" and self-distillation, where you train a model, throw away the later layers, reinitialize them, and retrain. And somewhat surprisingly, you often end up with a better model than if you'd just kept training the original one.

The way I came to understand it is through the lens of forgetting as a mechanism for escaping bad local structure. When you train a network end to end, the early layers learn features and the later layers learn how to use those features. But the later layers are very opportunistic. They'll latch onto whatever is easiest to exploit at the time, which often means spurious correlations or very specific, overfit combinations of features. And once they've committed to that, the gradients they send back to the early layers reinforce exactly those shortcuts. So the whole network gets locked into a solution that's kind of co-adapted and brittle.

When you reset the later layers, you keep the early features, which tend to be more general and more transferable, but you erase the specific way they were being combined. Now the new later layers have to relearn from scratch, but they're relearning on top of features that have already matured. So they can find a different, often simpler, mapping from those features to the output. And crucially, the early layers now get a fresh gradient signal that isn't tied to the old shortcuts, which lets them improve too.

So the broader framing we landed on is that forgetting isn't always a bad thing. We usually think of it as this failure mode, catastrophic forgetting, loss of information. But selective forgetting, where you throw away the parts of the model that are most likely to be overfit, can actually be a regularizer. It's a bit like iterated learning in the cognitive science literature, where knowledge gets transmitted through a bottleneck across generations and the stuff that survives is the stuff that's more compressible and more general.

One thing I'd emphasize is that this isn't a complete explanation. We can show empirically that the solutions after reinitialization generalize better and are in some sense "simpler," but the exact dynamics of why the later layers are the right place to forget, versus the early layers, is still partly intuition. The early layers forget less because they're farther from the loss and move more slowly, so they're naturally more stable, and the later layers are where most of the memorization lives. But I think there's a lot more to understand there.

r001.rationale: The response says fresh gradients can let early layers improve, but does not identify continued strengthening across repeated reinitializations as the experimentally favored explanation.

r002.rationale: It describes a fresh gradient signal after resetting later layers, but does not say that this signal is stronger than the one in a fully trained network.

r003.rationale: It calls early features general and transferable, but does not connect that generality to adapting across environments created by later-layer reinitializations.

astra-6.text:
One way to think about it is that the layers of a network are learning together, but they’re also learning from a moving target. Early in training, the later layers have to work with representations that are still quite poor. As the earlier layers improve, some of the choices the later layers made may no longer be particularly good, but ordinary training doesn’t necessarily undo them completely.

So if you keep the learned representations in the earlier layers and reinitialize the later layers, you give those later layers a chance to learn again from a much better starting point in terms of their inputs. You’re throwing away some of the dependence on that early training history while preserving useful features.

That’s an intuition rather than a complete explanation. You’re deliberately making the network worse immediately after the reset, but after retraining it can generalize better. The interesting question is which parts of the learned solution are worth preserving and which parts benefit from that fresh start.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier layers improve and their useful features are preserved, but it does not identify continued strengthening of those features as the experimentally favored explanation for gains from repeated resets.

r002.rationale: It does not state that resetting later layers lets a stronger training signal propagate back to earlier layers.

r003.rationale: It does not connect features that adapt across different reinitialization environments with greater generality.

sol-6.1.text:
My intuition is that it gives the network a chance to learn the later layers again using better features. Early in training, all the layers are changing at once. The later layers are learning from representations that are still developing, and some of those early choices can persist even after the representations improve.

If we keep the earlier layers and reinitialize the later ones, we preserve the useful features but give the network a fresh opportunity to combine them. So the second round of training starts from a different situation: the later layers have useful representations available right away.

That’s an intuition rather than a complete explanation, though. It doesn’t mean resetting layers will always help; which layers you reset and when you do it matter.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier features develop and are preserved, but does not identify continued strengthening of those features as the experimentally favored explanation.

r002.rationale: It does not mention a stronger training signal propagating back to earlier layers.

r003.rationale: It does not connect features’ ability to adapt across different later-layer reinitializations with greater generality.
